title: Memory management
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs probe contiguous vs non-contiguous allocation, fragmentation, and page-table address translation to test whether candidates understand how the OS packs processes into main memory.
company_notes: Cisco-style multi-selects on fixed partitioning often list that it suffers both internal and external fragmentation — the option candidates wrongly deselect.

phases.goal: Establish why the OS manages main memory, what degree of multiprogramming means, and how contiguous vs non-contiguous allocation families differ.

must_hit.point: Memory management keeps many processes in main memory so the CPU stays busy; the CPU only fetches instructions and data from registers, cache, and main memory, while disk is far slower.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states the goal as efficient use of main memory / keeping enough processes resident, and places disk below the register–cache–RAM hierarchy in speed.

must_hit.point: Degree of multiprogramming is the number of processes held in main memory at once; raising it improves CPU utilization until memory pressure causes thrashing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate defines degree of multiprogramming and links a higher count to a ready process being available when one blocks, with thrashing as the overload limit.

must_hit.point: Contiguous allocation gives each process one continuous block (fixed/static or variable/dynamic partitioning); non-contiguous scatters a process via paging, multilevel/inverted paging, segmentation, or segmented paging.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names both families and at least the main members: fixed and variable partitioning vs paging/segmentation variants.

probes: What is memory management trying to achieve, and what is degree of multiprogramming?
How do contiguous and non-contiguous allocation differ at a high level?

hints.1: Start from where the CPU can actually fetch instructions and why more resident processes help utilization.
hints.2: Define degree of multiprogramming, then split techniques into one continuous block vs scattered pieces.
hints.3: Goal: efficient RAM use so the CPU stays busy. Degree of multiprogramming = processes in main memory. Contiguous = fixed/variable partitions; non-contiguous = paging, multilevel/inverted paging, segmentation, segmented paging.

phases.goal: Explain fixed and variable partitioning, how paging and the MMU translate addresses, page-table entry bits, multilevel and inverted tables, and segmentation translation.

must_hit.point: Fixed partitioning divides memory into a fixed number of fixed-size partitions; each holds at most one process that must fit entirely in one partition, causing internal fragmentation, a hard process-size limit, a cap on multiprogramming, and external fragmentation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states fixed count and sizes, one process per partition, and lists the four limitations including both fragmentation types.

must_hit.point: Variable partitioning creates a partition to fit each process exactly at load time, removing internal fragmentation and fixed size/count limits, but holes produce external fragmentation as processes come and go.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts exact-fit partitions with hole-based external fragmentation and may name compaction or paging as remedies.

must_hit.point: Paging divides physical memory into fixed-size frames and logical memory into equal-size pages; a per-process page table maps page number to frame, and the MMU translates on every access, so there is no external fragmentation and only bounded internal fragmentation in the last page.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate equates page and frame size, describes non-contiguous frame placement via the page table/MMU, and states no external fragmentation with at most one partial last page.

must_hit.point: A logical address splits into page number and offset; the page table yields a frame number concatenated with the unchanged offset to form the physical address.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate walks page-number → page-table → frame-number | offset without rewriting the offset.

must_hit.point: Each page-table entry holds a frame number plus control bits: valid/invalid (present/absent), protection, reference, dirty/modified, and caching.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists frame number plus several of those control bits with their roles (e.g., dirty avoids writing back clean pages).

must_hit.point: Multilevel paging pages the page table so an outer table points to pages of the inner table and only needed portions stay in memory; an inverted page table has one system-wide entry per frame recording <process id, page number>, shrinking size but requiring search (sped up with hashing and the TLB).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts one-entry-per-page (per process) with hierarchical paging and with one-entry-per-frame inverted lookup.

must_hit.point: Segmentation splits a process into variable-size logical segments; the segment table stores base and limit, and offset must be less than limit or hardware raises a segmentation-fault trap; physical address is base + offset.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes (segment number, offset) → base/limit check → base + offset or trap.

probes: How do fixed and variable partitioning differ in fragmentation and limits on process size or count?
Walk a paging address translation from logical address through the page table to a physical address.
How does segmentation translate (segment number, offset), and what happens if the offset is out of range?

hints.1: Separate pre-cut fixed partitions from exact-fit dynamic ones, then pages/frames from logical segments.
hints.2: For paging: page number indexes the table to a frame; offset is unchanged. For segments: base + offset with a limit check.
hints.3: Fixed: both fragmentations and hard caps. Variable: holes/external only. Paging: page|offset → frame|offset via MMU; PTE has frame + valid/protection/reference/dirty/caching. Multilevel pages the table; inverted is one entry per frame. Segmentation: base/limit, trap if offset ≥ limit.

phases.goal: Compare placement algorithms, compaction versus paging as external-fragmentation fixes, and paging versus segmentation (including segmented paging).

must_hit.point: Among hole-placement algorithms, first fit takes the first large enough hole (fast, good general choice); next fit resumes from the last placement (spreads usage, can be worse than first fit); best fit takes the smallest fitting hole (least waste now, many tiny useless holes, slow full scan); worst fit takes the largest hole (usable remainder, consumes big holes, slow).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states each rule and its main trade-off without inventing extra algorithms.

must_hit.point: Compaction merges holes by sliding allocated blocks together but is expensive because it must pause and relocate processes; non-contiguous paging is the stronger fix that sidesteps external fragmentation entirely.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts costly relocation/compaction with paging removing the need to find one large contiguous hole.

must_hit.point: Paging uses fixed-size pages, is invisible to the programmer, and has only minor internal fragmentation; segmentation uses variable logical segments visible to the programmer and matching program structure, but suffers external fragmentation; segmented paging combines both for logical structure without external fragmentation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate hits fixed vs variable, programmer visibility, fragmentation contrast, and segmented paging as the hybrid.

must_hit.point: A normal page table has one entry per page per process and grows huge for large address spaces; an inverted table has one entry per physical frame for the whole system, dramatically smaller but slower to look up without hashing/TLB help.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts per-page indexing cost with per-frame search cost and the size win of inverted tables.

probes: When several holes fit a process, how do first, next, best, and worst fit differ?
Paging versus segmentation: what does each optimize for, and what fragmentation does each suffer?

hints.1: Think about which hole you pick now versus what leftover holes you leave behind.
hints.2: Pair placement-algorithm rules with compaction vs paging, then fixed invisible pages vs variable visible segments.
hints.3: First=first hole (fast); next=resume search; best=smallest hole (tiny leftovers); worst=largest hole. Compaction relocates; paging removes external fragmentation. Paging: minor internal; segmentation: external; segmented paging gets both benefits. Inverted: one entry per frame, search not index.

phases.goal: Apply fragmentation examples and the worked paging address-space numbers to check concrete understanding.

must_hit.point: Under fixed partitioning, a 6 MB process in an 8 MB partition wastes 2 MB as internal fragmentation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate computes leftover inside the partition as internal waste of 2 MB.

must_hit.point: With a 4 GB = 2^32 B logical space, 64 MB = 2^26 B physical space, and 4 KB = 2^12 B pages, the logical address is 32 bits, the physical address is 26 bits, and the offset is 12 bits.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate derives address widths from the given spaces and page size without changing the figures.

must_hit.point: In that worked example there are 2^20 pages and 2^14 frames; page-number bits are 20 and frame-number bits are 14; the page table has 2^20 entries and size 2^20 × 14 bits ≈ 2.5 MB.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states 2^20 / 2^14 / 20 / 14 and sizes the table as entries times frame-number bits ≈ 2.5 MB.

must_hit.point: A page-table entry stores the frame number (14 bits in the example), not the full physical address — the offset is not stored — so table size is entries times frame-number width, not times page size.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate refuses to multiply entries by page size or store the full physical address in each PTE.

probes: In fixed partitioning, what fragmentation occurs when a 6 MB process is placed in an 8 MB partition?
Given 4 GB logical, 64 MB physical, and 4 KB pages, how wide are page number, frame number, and the page table?

hints.1: Internal waste is leftover space inside an allocated partition or last page.
hints.2: Offset bits come from page size; page/frame count bits are address bits minus offset; PTE width is frame-number bits only.
hints.3: 6 MB in 8 MB → 2 MB internal. 32-bit logical, 26-bit physical, 12-bit offset → 2^20 pages, 2^14 frames, 20/14 bit fields, table ≈ 2.5 MB as 2^20 × 14 bits — not full physical addresses.

tradeoffs.topic: First fit vs next fit vs best fit vs worst fit
tradeoffs.strong_answer: First fit: first hole large enough — fast and a good general choice. Next fit: resume from last placement — spreads usage but can be worse than first fit. Best fit: smallest fitting hole — least waste now but many tiny useless holes and a slow full scan. Worst fit: largest hole — leaves a usable remainder but consumes big holes and is slow.

Compaction slides allocated blocks together to merge holes into one free region but must pause and relocate processes. Paging places pages in any free frames and sidesteps external fragmentation entirely.

Paging uses fixed-size pages, is invisible to the programmer, and suffers only minor internal fragmentation (last page). Segmentation uses variable-size logical segments visible to the programmer and matching code/stack/heap structure, but suffers external fragmentation. Segmented paging divides segments into pages to keep logical structure without external fragmentation.

tradeoffs.topic: Normal page table vs inverted page table
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Normal tables have one entry per page per process and become huge for large address spaces. An inverted table has one system-wide entry per physical frame recording <process id, page number>, much smaller but lookup is a search rather than an index, so hashing and the TLB are used to speed it up.

gotchas.trap: Deselecting that fixed partitioning suffers both internal and external fragmentation on a multi-select.
gotchas.correction: Fixed partitioning has internal waste inside oversized partitions and external waste when a free partition is too small for any waiting process — both apply.

gotchas.trap: Assuming variable partitioning eliminates all fragmentation.
gotchas.correction: It removes internal fragmentation and fixed size/count limits, but holes still cause external fragmentation.

gotchas.trap: Thinking paging still has external fragmentation like contiguous allocation.
gotchas.correction: Equal page and frame sizes mean any free frame fits any page — no external fragmentation; only the last page may be partly empty.

gotchas.trap: Storing a full physical address in each page-table entry, or sizing the table as entries × page size.
gotchas.correction: A PTE stores the frame number only (14 bits in the worked example); the offset is concatenated at translation time. Size is entries × frame-number width (≈ 2.5 MB for 2^20 × 14 bits).

gotchas.trap: Treating an inverted page table like an indexed per-page table.
gotchas.correction: Inverted tables have one entry per frame and must be searched for <process id, page number>; hashing and the TLB compensate for the slower lookup.
